item.title: Permit L in Vaud: validity 1 year and renewal up to 24 months
item.description: The L permit lasts a maximum of 1 year, renewable for a second year. After 24 months it passes to permit B. Complete guide for the Canton of Vaud.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit L: maximum validity of 1 year - Renewable for a second year - Maximum total: 24 months - Switch to permit B after 2 years
## Key facts - Permit type: L (short duration) - Initial duration: up to 1 year - Renewal: possible for 1 year - Total duration max: 2 years - Next step: Permit B (residence) - Authority: SEM (Secretariat of State for Migration)
The short-term permit, known as the L permit, is the main instrument for third-country nationals who intend to work in Switzerland for a limited period. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) defines the federal guidelines, which are applied by the various Cantons, including the specific procedure in the Canton of Vaud. The distinctive feature of this permit is its temporary nature, designed for defined work projects or for probationary periods before a professional stabilization.
The standard validity of the L permit is set at one year. This term is not fixed but represents the maximum limit for the first issue. The employer must be the applicant for the procedure, ensuring that the workplace is real and compliant with labour market regulations. Once the first year has expired, the holder may request a renewal for a second year, provided that the employment relationship continues and that there are no substantial changes in the contractual conditions or in the personal situation of the worker.
### The structure The distinction between the L permit and the B permit is not merely formal but has direct practical implications for the daily life and financial planning of those living in Switzerland. While the L permit is strictly tied to a specific employment relationship, the B permit offers greater autonomy. However, the transition is not automatic: it requires a conversion procedure that must be initiated before the expiration of the second year of the L permit.
### Implications for social security and taxation
During the period of the L permit, the worker is subject to the same social security regulations as any other resident. AVS/AI/IPG contributions are mandatory, with a rate of 5.3% paid by the employee and the same amount paid by the employer, for a total of 10.6%. Unemployment insurance (AD/AC) and mandatory daily allowance insurance for sickness and maternity (LAINF/LAA) also apply, with rates varying between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector.
Regarding professional pension schemes, the LPP/BVG comes into play for the portion of the salary that exceeds the coordination threshold. Contribution rates vary based on age: from 7% for those aged 25-34 up to 18% for those aged 55 and over. It is important to note that, despite being a short-term permit, work performed under an L permit generates social security contributions which, in the event of moving abroad, can be refunded or retained based on bilateral agreements.
On the fiscal level, a worker residing in Vaud is subject to the three-tier tax system: federal, cantonal, and communal. The Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV) manages direct federal tax (IFD) and VAT, while cantonal and communal administrations apply their own multipliers. Residence in Switzerland, even temporary, triggers the obligation to file a tax return. The cost of living and budget management must take these withholdings into account, as they significantly impact the monthly net income.
### Transition scenarios
If the employer decides not to renew the contract at the end of the first year, the worker finds themselves in a delicate position. Without a new contract to justify the renewal of the L permit, residency is at risk. In such cases, the search for a new job must take place within the timeframes established by law to avoid losing the right of residence. The flexibility of the Swiss labor market, while high, does not automatically guarantee permit continuity if the employment link is broken. Advance planning, including verifying the requirements for a B permit, is recommended to avoid interruptions in social security and health coverage.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). To properly manage the transition from an L permit to a B permit, it is essential to adhere to precise timing. The conversion application must be submitted before the expiration of the second year of the L permit. Delaying this procedure may result in the loss of insurance coverage and the need to restart the process from the beginning.
### Step-by-step procedure
1. Document verification: ensure you have an updated employment contract, salary certificates, and proof of residence in Switzerland. 2. Application submission: contact the migration office of the Canton of Vaud with complete documentation. The employer must co-sign the request. 3. Health insurance: verify that your LAMal coverage is active and that the chosen deductible is adequate for your budget. Coverage is mandatory within 3 months of arrival and must remain valid throughout the entire period of residence. 4. Bank account: if you do not already have one, open an account in Switzerland to manage tax and social security withholdings. Current accounts are managed by national banks and must comply with anti-money laundering regulations.
### Useful tools for planning
To accurately calculate your net income and the taxes due in Vaud, it is useful to use tax simulation tools. These tools allow you to see how cantonal and municipal tax rates influence your payslip. Additionally, it is important to monitor the cost of living, which varies from one region to another, to adapt your standard of living to your net income.
Pension provision is another aspect to consider in the long term. Even if the L permit is short-term, contributions paid to LPP/BVG are accumulated and can be transferred or refunded according to federal laws. Always check the available options to avoid losing acquired rights.
For those in a transitional situation, the support of a tax consultant or a union can be valuable. However, the first line of defense remains understanding your legal and tax obligations. Switzerland offers a transparent system, but it requires that residents know the rules of the game.

The sustainability of the loan is assessed on the basis of the ratio between installments and disposable income, according to criteria established by the supervisory authorities and Swiss banking rules. ### Prices and Funds ## The Practical Impact of Tax and Banking Choices
Buying a home in the Canton of Zug requires planning that takes into account not only the property price but also all additional expenses. The property transfer tax, present in every Swiss canton, is regulated at the cantonal level with a multiplier that can vary between municipalities. This means the tax amount depends on the exact location of the property: two municipalities within the same canton may apply different rates. For the buyer, it is important to inquire at the relevant municipal administration before proceeding with the purchase.
Notary fees, on the other hand, are set at the federal level and do not vary between cantons. They include the cost of the notarial deed and related taxes, and are added to the purchase price of the home. This means that, in addition to the equity and mortgage, the buyer must consider an additional financial burden that is not always calculated upfront. The combination of property transfer tax and notary fees can represent a significant portion of the total cost, especially in a canton like Zug where real estate prices are already high.

The sustainability of the mortgage is a crucial aspect evaluated by Swiss banks when granting a loan. The ratio between installments and available income must remain within thresholds set by supervisory regulations, ensuring that the buyer does not impose an excessive burden on their budget. The required equity varies depending on the type of mortgage and the policy subscribed to, but generally, banks require a minimum that covers a significant portion of the property price.
This mechanism encourages the buyer to plan their resources in advance, evaluating the possibility of increasing available equity or reducing the mortgage request. Mortgage sustainability is not just a matter of amount: banks also assess income stability, the duration of the employment contract, and the ability to maintain installments even in the event of unforeseen circumstances. This prudent approach by the Swiss banking system aims to contain the risk of insolvency, protecting both the buyer and the bank itself.

item.title: Federal Council rejects the UDC initiative on borders
item.description: The Federal Council recommends rejecting the UDC initiative on borders. High costs, damage to the economy and risks for Schengen have been detected.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - The Federal Council rejects the SVP border initiative - High costs and damage to the Swiss economy identified - The executive warns of risks to Schengen and Dublin - Alternative measures on the way through the European Pact
## Key facts - Initiative: Stop abuses in asylum - Daily border crossings: 2.2 million - Cost of leaving Schengen: 5.8 to 16.1 billion - Maximum asylum limit: 5,000 people
The Federal Council has officially recommended that Parliament reject the popular initiative promoted by the SVP for border protection, formally named Stop abuses in asylum. The Swiss executive expressed a clear rejection of the proposal, highlighting a series of significant critical issues that could affect the entire national territory. According to the government's assessment, the implementation of the new measures would entail very high costs, a deterioration of the country's welfare, a weakening of internal security, and severe damage to Switzerland's traditional humanitarian policy. Furthermore, the executive reiterated that the text would not even be suitable for effectively curbing the phenomenon of irregular migration and cross-border crime. Specifically, the initiative requires systematically controlling all incoming people, fully manning border crossings, and turning back those who do not meet entry conditions, while introducing a maximum cap of 5,000 asylum grants per year. For those staying irregularly, the text requires a notification obligation, the nullity of employment contracts, exclusion from social and health insurance, and the obligation to leave the territory within 90 days.
### Impacts on daily mobility The repercussions of permanent and systematic controls would inevitably reflect on traffic and the management of Swiss customs checkpoints. The Confederation registers approximately 2.2 million border crossings daily and the presence of many hundreds of thousands of cross-border commuters. Consequently, the execution of fixed and systematic checks would heavily burden the national economy and traffic fluidity, generating billions of francs in congestion costs especially in border regions. The government emphasizes that it would be essential to significantly increase border protection personnel, generating a further increase in public spending. Current customs procedures, the executive recalls, are already based on checks tailored to the situation and risks, which can be intensified as needed without resorting to permanent blockades of internal borders. To delve deeper into the general economic impact and the management of daily expenses, you can consult the resources dedicated to the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in Switzerland. ### Security and Schengen Consequences
A central aspect of the analysis conducted by the Federal Council concerns the strategic link between Switzerland and European cooperation agreements. Accepting the initiative would concretely jeopardize the Confederation's association with the Schengen and Dublin system. The potential abandonment of this regulatory and security framework would weaken the country's internal protection, as Switzerland would lose immediate access to shared European search databases. Furthermore, Swiss authorities would find themselves in a position of having to independently re-examine all applications rejected by other Dublin member states, without retaining the power to transfer applicants to the competent European countries. This situation would lead to a significant and predictable increase in the number of applications handled directly at the national level. To support this assessment, the government cites an official report commissioned by the National Council, according to which the annual costs resulting from the abandonment of Schengen and Dublin would range between a minimum of 5.8 billion and a maximum of 16.1 billion Swiss francs.
### Analysis of Quantitative and Humanitarian Limits
The proposal to set a maximum limit of 5,000 asylum grants per year conflicts with obligations arising from international law. To avoid violations of signed treaties, the Confederation would still be required to examine each individual asylum application separately, making it impossible to proceed with automatic rejection and repatriation of applicants. People fleeing armed conflict zones would no longer be able to obtain provisional admission, thus calling into question Switzerland's historic humanitarian tradition. On the integration front, the text under examination would make it almost impossible for individuals with prolonged stays to achieve financial independence, with the concrete risk of heavily overburdening cantonal structures dedicated to emergency relief. Nevertheless, the executive recognizes the need to intervene in the migration sector, aiming to curb secondary migration movements within the Schengen area through the coordinated application of measures provided for by the European Pact on Migration and Asylum, in which Switzerland actively participates.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Legislative Outlook and Cantonal Interventions Despite the strongly negative opinion expressed by the Federal Council regarding the SVP popular initiative, the executive branch and cantonal administrations agree on the need to implement targeted reforms in the migration management sector. In this scenario, the Federal Department of Justice and Police has initiated preparatory work to define, in close collaboration with the Cantons, new legislative amendments. The primary objective of these regulatory interventions is to tangibly relieve the national asylum system and overall raise security levels within the sector. The Cantons and federal authorities therefore continue to monitor the evolution of the regulatory framework, evaluating alternative administrative tools to address the challenges related to migration flows without compromising economic balances and the free movement of cross-border commuters. Final decisions will now be submitted to the Federal Parliament, which will have to discuss the rejection recommendation formulated by the executive and schedule the next institutional steps.
### Operational References for Citizens For those who live and work in Swiss territory, the evolution of the political and regulatory debate on security, cross-border commuting, and public finance requires constant monitoring of federal provisions. The reforms announced by the Federal Department of Justice and Police and the Cantons could impact administrative management and public expenditure planning in the medium term. It is advisable to regularly check your social security and contribution status through the available official tools. item.title: SNB: fixed rates at 0.0% and future forecasts
item.description: The Swiss National Bank is preparing for the economic exam with rates at 0.0% and inflation in Switzerland rising to 0.8% in August.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The SNB will hold its third annual review of the economic and monetary situation - Experts unanimous: policy rate will remain unchanged at 0.0% - Inflation in Switzerland rose to 0.8% in August - 2027 forecasts split between 0.0% and 0.75%
## Key facts - Institution: SNB - Review date: Thursday - Current policy rate: 0.0% - August inflation: 0.8% - July inflation: 0.4% - SNB target range: 0% and 2% - 2027 rate spread: 0.00 to 0.75% - Chairman of the institution: Martin Schlegel
The Swiss National Bank (SNB) is preparing for its third annual review of the economic and monetary situation, scheduled for Thursday in Bern. Economic experts are absolutely unanimous in believing that the policy rate will remain unchanged at 0.0% during this monetary policy appointment. Despite the recent increase recorded in Switzerland by inflation, which rose to 0.8% in August from 0.4% in July, analysts agree that there are currently no prerequisites for an immediate intervention on the cost of borrowing.
### The inflation and interest rate framework
The price increase recorded in recent months continues to remain stably within the target range defined by the SNB itself, specifically a band between 0% and 2%. Consequently, price dynamics show no alarm signals that would justify an immediate monetary tightening. The current situation sees the Swiss central bank moving in an international context characterized by different moves by other major global monetary authorities.
### Decisions of foreign central banks
Last week, the European Central Bank (ECB) proceeded with a rate hike, while this Wednesday the Federal Reserve implemented its first increase. Inevitably, faced with these international movements, the question that operators and analysts are asking concerns the future moves of the SNB in the coming months and quarters. Although Thursday's review holds no surprises regarding the current level of the policy rate, general attention inevitably shifts toward the coming quarters, where the real question for economists is no longer whether there will be interventions, but when they will be implemented. The estimates prepared by experts for the coming quarters and the end of 2027 diverge widely, drawing a range for the SNB's policy rate from 0.00% to 0.75%. This strong divergence of opinions among financial analysts highlights the uncertainty linked to the evolution of national and international macroeconomic factors in the coming years. The research institute BAK Economics hypothesizes a first increase in the cost of money as early as December, while other operators in the financial sector shift the forecast for the first increase starting from March 2027.
### Economic pressure factors
At the root of these upward forecasts are very precise elements: rising inflation, the trend towards a weaker franc, and the overall recovery of the economy. Under these operating conditions, the strongly expansionary stance of monetary policy adopted so far would no longer be considered necessary, making a gradual normalization of interest rates appropriate. In recent months, the Swiss currency has recorded a noticeable weakening that certainly offers a competitive advantage to the export economy, but at the same time makes imported goods decidedly more expensive, starting with energy.
### The impact of the franc and the SNB's reaction
A less strong franc generates inevitable additional inflationary pressure originating from abroad. As long as the Swiss currency maintains underlying robustness and domestic price increases remain low, the SNB can afford to keep the rate at 0.0%. However, the longer and more intensely the franc weakens, the greater the pressure on imported prices becomes. In this scenario, several specialists predict that the institution led by Martin Schlegel could primarily use foreign currency sales as a complementary intervention tool, favoring the appreciation of the franc and containing external inflationary pressure.
### The role of reserves and the rate differential
The management of the huge accumulated foreign exchange reserves offers the SNB considerable leeway to intervene in the currency markets. As Renato Flückiger of Valiant Bank points out, this aspect takes on particular significance in the event that the interest rate differential with cross-border countries should continue to widen further over the coming months.

item.description: The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal of prio.swiss against the hospital list of the Canton of Switzerland. Only targeted appeals are possible.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Appeal dismissed by the Federal Administrative Court - Insurers cannot challenge the entire hospital list - It is only possible to appeal individual planning decisions - The court's decision is final and without appeal
## Key facts - Appellant body: Association of Swiss Health Insurers (prio.swiss) - Court: Federal Administrative Court (FAC) in St. Gallen - Canton concerned: Canton of Schwyz - Scope: List of hospitals for acute somatic care - Outcome: Appeal dismissed
Health insurers do not have the legal standing to file an appeal against a canton's hospital list in its entirety. In a published ruling, the Federal Administrative Court formally dismissed the application filed by the trade association. The legal dispute originated from the appeal submitted by the Association of Swiss Health Insurers (prio.swiss) to the Federal Administrative Court (FAC) in St. Gallen. The subject of the dispute concerned the list of hospitals for acute somatic care drawn up by the State Council of the Canton of Schwyz. Based on what emerged in the legal claims, the insurers sought the complete annulment of the hospital list. The claim put forward aimed to obtain the referral of the entire act to the Schwyz executive, so that the latter could proceed with the drafting of a new comprehensive hospital planning for the cantonal territory. However, the judges based in St. Gallen examined the issue and established an opposite principle, rejecting the request for total annulment.
### The assessment of the federal administrative judges
According to the orientation expressed by the Federal Administrative Court, a hospital list cannot in any way constitute the object of a global or collective challenge. In the grounds written in support of the judgment, the FAC clarified that a list of hospital facilities does not represent a single and indivisible administrative act. On the contrary, it constitutes a coordinated set of distinct service mandates entrusted to individual facilities operating within a canton, namely hospitals, maternity homes and nursing homes. For this reason, the judicial system excludes the possibility of contesting the entire planning framework with a single general appeal. Insurers nevertheless retain the prerogative to act in the appropriate venues, but through different methods compared to what was attempted against the Canton of Schwyz. The practical implications arising from the ruling of the Federal Administrative Tribunal outline a well-defined framework regarding the relations between trade associations in the insurance sector and cantonal governments on health matters. The decision establishes a clear line of demarcation on the methods for controlling regional hospital planning. Industry operators cannot undertake massive legal action to overturn the entire acute somatic care planning network decided by a cantonal executive. On the contrary, the protection of the economic and managerial interests of health insurers must necessarily take place through targeted and punctual challenges.
### Analysis of appeal procedures and operational alternatives
The procedural rules set by the judges in St. Gallen require insurers to change their strategy in examining the health planning measures issued by the Cantons. In detail, the possibility of using judicial instruments to contest cantonal administrative decisions must translate into the appeal of individual specific measures. When a trade association identifies critical issues in the distribution of service mandates, legal action cannot target the general act of the Council of State, but must focus on the individual mandates assigned to well-identified structures, such as specific hospitals, individual maternity homes, or individual nursing homes. This restrictive principle protects the stability of local public health planning, preventing entire lists of regional health structures from being blocked or called into question by a global appeal filed by insurance organizations. To verify how these dynamics reflect on the system and consult regulatory details or the overall impact on costs, it is useful to consult the overview on the cost of living in Switzerland (nav:cost-of-living) to have a clear picture of health and administrative expenses in the country.

The judges of St. Gallen have expressly stressed that the decision is not susceptible to further encumbrance and cannot in any way be appealed before the Federal Court of Lausanne. This means that the judicial process for the global challenge of the cantonal hospital lists is definitively interrupted at the TAF level, confirming the restrictive orientation adopted regarding the right of appeal of trade associations.

For operators in the sector and trade associations that intend to monitor or challenge the health planning acts issued by the cantonal governments, the way forward requires a detailed and targeted analysis of the individual administrative measures. ## In brief - Suissenégoce rejects new profit taxes - Risk of oil shortage in Switzerland ruled out - 50% of the petrol price derives from taxes
## Key facts - Association: Suissenégoce - Sector: Commodity trading and shipping - Representative: Florence Schurch - Policy: Karin Keller-Sutter - Refinery: Cressier - Refinery coverage: 30%
Suissenégoce, the association of Swiss companies active in commodity trading and shipping, has expressed strong opposition against any hypothesis of additional taxation targeting the profits of companies in the sector. In an interview with the Awp agency, Secretary General Florence Schurch addressed recent political discussions and international economic tensions directly involving Switzerland.
Taxing the profits of companies active in the oil and commodity sector more heavily does not represent an effective solution, according to the association, since the companies involved already pay huge sums in taxes, quantifiable in hundreds of millions of francs. The head of the Federal Department of Finance, Karin Keller-Sutter, herself highlighted how the Confederation managed to close its budget thanks to the tax revenue generated in Geneva.
### The role of companies and pump prices
Companies in the sector operate on the global market and are remunerated for their brokerage and supply activities, but cannot be held responsible for world geopolitical events or fluctuations in fuel prices. The price applied at the petrol pump depends on multiple complex factors, including refining costs, transport expenses, the exchange rate and excise duties applied by government authorities. The tensions recorded in the Middle East have caused a drastic reduction in oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and, more recently, through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, blocked by Houthi activities. Despite this complex scenario, there is no risk of energy shortages in Switzerland. This security is guaranteed on one hand by the country's accumulated strategic reserves and on the other by Switzerland's ability to absorb price increases with greater ease compared to other nations.
### Supply Strategies and Alternative Routes
When oil becomes less accessible in certain geographical areas, the task of traders consists in diversifying supply sources, turning to alternative producing countries such as Norway, Africa, or the United States. The real risk for the market is not the physical lack of the raw material, but rather the upward price dynamics due to lower global availability. Tariffs depend entirely on market trends and are subject to random factors that make it impossible to predict the maximum level prices could reach.
Regarding transport routes, logistical difficulties in the Persian Gulf force traders to transport oil by truck across the Arabian Peninsula to reach the Red Sea and load it onto ships, as the pipeline crossing Saudi Arabia has been hit by bombings. This extraordinary logistical chain and growing insurance costs inevitably contribute to pushing final energy prices upwards, while the duration of these price hikes represents the true critical issue for the economic system.

A concrete example involves the Cressier refinery in the Canton of Neuchatel, which supplies about 30% of the national fuel demand and for which the Confederation recently authorized a withdrawal from strategic reserves to cope with transport difficulties.
### Mitigation measures and fuel taxation
The logistical situation is also aggravated by internal factors, such as water levels in the Rhine River that are too low to allow full loading of vessels used for the transport of fossil energy. In this context, if fuel prices were to rise excessively, the federal government has the power to intervene by reducing the tax burden on petroleum products. ## In a nutshell - Permit C: permanent residence for foreign residents in Switzerland - Requirements: 10 years of residence (5 for EU/EFTA citizens) - Key factors: integration, language and absence of social aid - Procedure: application submitted to the authorities of the Canton of Zug
## Key facts Permission: Address C Standard residence: 10 years EU/EFTA Residence: 5 years Canton of reference: Zug Requirements: Integration, language, financial stability
Residence permit C represents the highest degree of stability for a foreign citizen residing in the Canton of Zug and, more generally, in Swiss territory. This residence permit, managed according to the SEM directives, makes it possible to almost totally equate the rights of the resident with those of the Swiss citizen, eliminating the need for periodic renewals typical of the B permit. To obtain it, the applicant must meet strict criteria related to the length of stay and personal conduct.
### Time requirements and access The general rule is that a foreign national can apply for the C permit after 10 years of uninterrupted residence in Switzerland. However, for citizens belonging to the EU/EFTA States, this period is reduced to 5 years, facilitating access to permanent residence. In the Canton of Zug, as in the rest of the Confederation, obtaining this permit is not automatic, but depends on the verification of specific integration and stability criteria.
Integration Obtaining the C permit in the Canton of Zug brings significant changes to the resident's daily and legal life. One of the main advantages is independence from the employment contract: unlike the B permit, which is often linked to a specific employer or the availability of employment, the C permit does not expire and does not require the employment contract to be updated for its maintenance. This ensures greater professional flexibility and superior psychological security for those who decide to invest long-term in the canton's economic fabric.
### Tax and Social Security Implications From a tax perspective, a resident with a C permit is fully integrated into Switzerland's three-tier system: direct federal tax (managed by the AFC/ESTV), cantonal tax, and municipal tax. In the Canton of Zug, known for its competitive tax policy, the cantonal and municipal taxes are calculated by applying a specific multiplier, which varies depending on the municipality of residence. This system makes it essential to monitor one's tax residence to optimize the overall tax burden.
On the social security front, the holder of a C permit continues to pay mandatory AVS/AI/IPG contributions (5.3% borne by the employee) and unemployment insurance AD/AC. The stability of domicile also facilitates the planning of professional pension LPP/BVG, where contributions vary based on age (from 7% for 25-34 year olds up to 18% for those over 55). Those holding a C permit can also manage their third pillar 3a with greater peace of mind, an essential tool for reducing taxable income and supplementing future pensions. The procedure for requesting the C residence permit in the Canton of Zug requires careful preparation of documentation to avoid delays or rejections. The first step consists of verifying that the required number of years of residence has been reached (10 years for non-EU citizens, 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens). Once the time requirement is met, the applicant must submit a formal application to the competent cantonal office.
### Operational steps for the application The process generally unfolds in the following phases:
- Document collection: it is necessary to provide proof of uninterrupted residence, updated criminal record certificates, and proof of integration. - Language demonstration: the applicant must certify knowledge of one of the national languages (German, in this case, as Zug is a German-speaking canton) through recognized certifications. - Financial verification: the authority checks for the absence of outstanding debts or the use of social assistance. - Submission and waiting: once the application is sent, the cantonal authority evaluates the applicant's profile and decides on the issuance of the permit.
There are cases of early issuance of the C permit, usually linked to particular merits, exceptional integration, or close family ties, although the criteria remain rigorous. The Federal Council has submitted a credit request to Parliament as part of the second supplementary budget, forecasting an increase of nearly one billion francs for the armed forces. This decision, already anticipated in August, responds to a worsening threat situation in Europe and strong tension affecting the armaments market. The executive's goal is to guarantee production capacities and ensure that delivery terms for systems deemed urgently necessary are respected, in line with the 2026 armament program.
### Detail of military investments
The breakdown of the 970 million francs allocated to the army is defined as follows: 650 million francs are planned for the purchase of medium-range ground-to-air defense systems, while 250 million are destined for short-range systems. A further 60 million francs will be used for the acquisition of a partially mobile medium-range radar, while 10 million francs are allocated for specific defense systems against mini-drones.
In addition to military spending, the government has requested further funds for various emergencies and commitments. 54 million francs have been allocated to support farms that suffered damage from drought during the summer. Regarding security linked to international events, 20 million francs are planned to cover 80% of the costs incurred by the Cantons of Geneva, Vaud, Valais, and Ticino for the G7 summit in Evian and the OSCE ministerial conference, which will be held in Lugano in December. Finally, 0.7 million francs are destined for Swiss company to reimburse the overnight stay expenses of air traffic security guards between 2016 and 2024. The impact of these decisions is directly reflected in the financial management of the Confederation and the organization of security in the involved Cantons. The Federal Council's request is not limited to immediate credits, but includes new commitment credits to allow the State to assume contractual obligations that extend beyond the current year. In particular, 100 million francs have been requested for urgent interventions in the real estate sector, aimed at improving the army's self-protection, 13.6 million for a portfolio management system for the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport (DDPS), and 15.8 million for the implementation of the cell broadcast alarm system.

For the residents and administrations of the Cantons of Ticino, Valais, Vaud, and Geneva, the federal intervention of 20 million francs represents a partial tax relief, covering 80% of the security costs for international summits. Without this contribution, the financial burden for organizing the OSCE conference in Lugano and the G7 in Evian would fall entirely on the cantonal budgets. This cost-sharing mechanism highlights how events of national or international importance require financial coordination between Bern and the Cantons.
On the infrastructural level, an additional credit of 5 million francs is planned for the Railway Infrastructure Fund (RIF), destined for the completion works of the New Railway Link through the Alps (NRLA). It is important to emphasize that this specific funding will not weigh on the Confederation's budget, as it is guaranteed directly by the RIF. This scenario differs from the credits for the army or agriculture, which instead impact State expenditures. From an accounting point of view, considering a credit carry-over of 23.6 million francs from 2025, the overall operation of the second supplement will lead to increased expenditures of 1.068 billion francs. ### Characteristics and limits of the L permit The temporary nature of this permit implies that it is not intended for those seeking immediate stable residence, but for those undertaking fixed-term assignments. The one-year time limit is mandatory for the initial validity. Since the permit is tied to the employer, the potential termination of the contractual relationship before the expiration of the title may affect the validity of the stay itself. ## In brief - Severe increase in housing shortage - Lowest point overcome - 45,000 units in 2026 - 50,000 units in 2027
## Key facts - Study published by: Wüest Partner - Net increase in 2024: 40,000 homes according to FSO - Estimated increase for 2025: 39,000 homes - Forecast for 2026: around 45,000 housing units - Forecast for 2027: around 50,000 housing units
In a context characterised by strong population growth in Switzerland, a significant housing shortage is currently being recorded, but the situation may improve soon, at least in some regions of the country. This is the main conclusion of a study published by the Wüest Partner real estate consultancy firm. According to the research, the lowest point in housing construction in Switzerland should now have been overcome. The company is forecasting around 45,000 housing units in 2026 and around 50,000 housing units in 2027.
To provide a direct comparison, it is worth looking at the data provided by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), according to which the net increase in 2024 was only 40,000 homes. As for the current year, 2025, the estimates produced by Wüest Partner indicate a further decline to just 39,000 homes, effectively representing the lowest level recorded since 2009. This prolonged slowdown has exacerbated tensions in the Swiss real estate market, pushing up demand and drastically reducing the options available to those looking for a home.
### The causes of the construction slowdown
The sharp increase in housing production expected in the coming years should at least slightly alleviate the housing shortage throughout Switzerland by the end of 2027. According to Wüest Partner's analysis, the concrete foundations for this future recovery were laid several years ago. In 2020, vacant apartments, which had increased for consecutive years, began to decline rapidly. At the same time, the market value of residential properties rose sharply.
These favourable market conditions created strong incentives for new housing projects, stimulating further real estate development initiatives. However, from the initial project to the delivery of the finished house, several years regularly pass. Among the main reasons for this wait are the increased complexity in planning and building new homes caused by additional building regulations, rising construction costs and interest rate trends. These factors have temporarily acted as a brake on the sector, but in the meantime many projects developed since 2020 have passed the preliminary stages and are now in an advanced phase, close to completion. The recovery of the real estate and construction market will not be distributed uniformly across the entire national territory, but will follow a gradual and differentiated progression depending on the region. In fact, during 2026, the recovery will remain predominantly localized at the regional level. Housing production is expected to exceed the long-term average, particularly in individual cantons of French-speaking Switzerland and Alpine regions, offering a first glimmer of relief in well-defined geographical areas.
The situation is destined to evolve further in the following year. In 2027, the recovery will clearly gain greater geographical breadth, involving a larger number of territories. In particular, a strong increase in the number of available housing units is expected in Thurgau, Geneva, Valais, and Neuchâtel. Large parts of the Swiss Plateau should also significantly benefit from this positive development, offering new opportunities for those seeking stable housing solutions.
### Regional differences and prospects in major centers
Despite growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027, significant territorial disparities persist that require attention. In approximately half of Swiss cantons, housing production will continue to remain below the long-term average. Real estate experts strongly emphasize that a generalized easing of housing tensions is not yet on the horizon for the entire country.
The situation is expected to remain particularly difficult and complex, especially in major urban centers, where demographic pressure and housing demand remain high. Furthermore, a key point highlighted by analysts concerns current construction applications: these do not currently forecast further acceleration in housing production for 2028, confirming that the market must proceed with caution and that normalization will take time.

The Confederation's expert group for economic forecasts published an update of its economic estimates for Switzerland in Bern on September 17, 2026. According to the report finalized on September 8, 2026, the Swiss economy is showing a recovery phase with an upward revision of gross domestic product growth for the current year. Growth of 1.7% is now expected for the current year, a figure significantly higher than the previous June forecast which indicated 0.9%. For 2027, however, the estimate remains unchanged at 1.6% net of sporting events. Swiss GDP recently recorded a strong increase, driven in the second quarter of 2026 by an extraordinary momentum equal to 1.5%.
### Sectoral dynamics of GDP The growth recorded in the second quarter of 2026 was broadly supported both at the sectoral level and from the demand side, although experts warn that this may be an overestimate of the underlying economic momentum. Indeed, almost half of this growth is attributable to the added value of the chemical and pharmaceutical industry, a sector historically characterized by strong fluctuations, accompanied by a marked increase in exports. In light of these factors, the Confederation's experts expect a reversal of the trend for the second half of the year. Despite this, the economic situation remains essentially on a recovery path and the excellent performance of the first half justifies the positive revision for the whole of 2026. Foreign trade is expected to contribute to a greater extent than June forecasts, supported by the positive economic trend so far, the slightly better global economic context and the recent depreciation of the Swiss franc, which facilitates export sectors particularly exposed to exchange rate fluctuations. Domestic demand instead continues with a moderate progression, while the greater exploitation of productive capacities favors investment activities and private consumption continues to grow in a controlled manner. The forecasts drawn up by the group of experts outline an overall stable economic scenario for the Swiss labour market, with direct repercussions on employment and price stability. The favourable economic trend is reflected in a gradual decrease in the unemployment rate, expected at 3.1% in the annual average for 2026 and forecast to fall further to 3.0% for 2027, confirming previous estimates without significant changes. On the inflation front, despite recent increases, prices remained at moderate levels until recently. Futures markets also indicate a possible drop in oil prices in the coming months, leading experts to confirm an average annual inflation rate of 0.6% for both 2026 and 2027.
### Growth scenarios and international recovery A further recovery in global demand is expected for 2027, driven mainly by European countries and first and foremost by Germany, whose exit from the phase of weakness in recent years will offer decisive support to the Swiss economy. GDP, adjusted for sporting events, is expected to grow by 1.6%. However, significant cyclical risks remain linked to international geopolitical and commercial factors. The conflict in the Middle East represents an element of strong uncertainty for the global economy: if the price of oil were to remain at high levels, it could weigh heavily on energy costs and push inflation upwards even in Switzerland. Given the very low inventories in Europe, further price increases cannot be ruled out even for natural gas. Added to this are uncertainties regarding trade policy and US import tariffs, which for now are assumed to remain at current levels but remain subject to possible future adjustments, including developments linked to the investigation launched on March 11, 2026 by the United States into alleged overcapacity in the industrial production of several States, including Switzerland. ## Key facts - Voting date: September 27, 2026 - gfs.bern poll period: September 2-9, 2026 - Interviewed sample: 12,916 voters - Margin of error: +/-2.8 percentage points - Support for neutrality initiative: 34% - Opponents of neutrality initiative: 63% - Undecided on neutrality initiative: 3% - Support for food initiative: 33% - Opponents of food initiative: 64% - Undecided on food initiative: 3%
About ten days before the federal votes on September 27, 2026, the neutrality initiative is in a difficult position and heading towards a ballot defeat. According to the second poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SSR), conducted by the gfs.bern research institute between September 2 and 9 among a sample of 12,916 voters with a margin of error between +/-2.8 percentage points, 63% of the electorate plans to reject the text launched by Pro Switzerland. Only 34% support the proposal and 3% remain undecided, while the no front has lost nine percentage points in a month.
### Support dynamics and political orientation The advance of the no vote is observed homogeneously throughout the federal territory. Even within the Swiss People's Party (SVP), which is the only party supporting the initiative, approval of the text has dropped by nine percentage points in a month, standing at 77%. gfs.bern political scientist Lukas Golder observes that the issue is more open than expected within the centrist electorate, as it is not one of the party's preferred topics, unlike migration or relations with the European Union where the base lines up more solidly. Voters of all other parties plan to reject the text increasingly clearly, while people without party affiliation have moved into the no camp, leaving in favor only those who harbor distrust towards the government, albeit with scarce support.
### Geographic and territorial evolution The gap between city and countryside, which had clearly emerged in the first poll, has progressively narrowed over the weeks preceding the popular consultation on September 27, 2026. By now, the initiative calling for the inclusion of a restrictive conception of neutrality in the Constitution is widely rejected even in the rural areas of Switzerland. From an argumentative standpoint, those who oppose perpetual neutrality anchored in the Constitution hold a clear advantage, since more than two-thirds of the respondents fear that the text could harm the country's security, limiting Switzerland's ability to cooperate with other states in this specific area. The definitive projection by gfs.bern political scientists clearly indicates that a rejection of the initiative represents the most likely scenario for this round of voting. ## Analysis of voting dynamics and comparison with the food initiative
The federal votes of September 27, 2026 present a complex picture involving multiple items submitted to a popular vote. Alongside the debate on Swiss neutrality, which aims to enshrine a stricter and more restrictive conception in the Constitution, the electorate's attention is also polarized on the initiative asking the Confederation to promote the production and consumption of plant-based foods. This second text has also seen a drastic decrease in support compared to the previous survey conducted by the gfs.bern institute on behalf of SSR.
### The text on plant-based food While in mid-August the supporting and opposing camps were still neck and neck in the public debate, almost two-thirds of the people interviewed, equal to 64%, now intend to vote no ahead of the September 27, 2026 deadline. Only 33% support the plant-based food initiative, while the share of undecided voters stands at 3%. This drastic trend reversal highlights how the information campaign and political debate have eroded initial consensus, shifting the absolute majority of voters toward the rejection of the federal regulatory proposal.
### Behavior of the diaspora and political parties An element of particular interest emerging from the second poll concerns the Fifth Switzerland, namely Swiss citizens residing abroad. A month ago the diaspora was in favor of the food initiative, but currently opposes it by a large majority with 59% against. Nonetheless, the text maintains higher support within this specific electorate, where 37% declared their intention to vote yes and 4% remain undecided. Experts explain this phenomenon by recalling that the diaspora historically tends to vote more in favor of ecological issues and is simultaneously less involved in national debates focused on the technical shortcomings of the text. Regarding Swiss political forces, the Greens electorate represents the only exception in the party landscape, continuing to support the food initiative with a percentage of 78%. Conversely, sympathizers of the Social Democratic Party (SP) and the Green Liberal Party (GLP), who at the beginning of the campaign showed significant openness, have changed their voting orientation over the weeks.

item.title: Cyber insurance growing in 2025 in Switzerland
item.description: In 2025, cyber insurance in Switzerland recorded strong growth: 72,000 insured companies and 480,000 individuals, according to ASA data.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Growth of cyber insurance in Switzerland in 2025 - Insured companies rose to 72,000, a 7% increase compared to the previous year - Strong growth among private individuals: +18% to 480,000 insured
## Key facts - Association: Swiss Insurance Association (SIA) - Reference year: 2025 - Insured companies: 72,000 - Company growth: 7% - Insured private individuals: 480,000 - Private growth: 18% - Private premiums: 29 million CHF - Business premiums: 153 million CHF - Insured Swiss companies: approximately 11% - Future event: Cyber Insurance Summit 2026 in Bern on November 5th
Cyber insurance, meaning insurance products that protect individuals and businesses from damages caused by cyberattacks or digital system issues, is experiencing a marked growth phase in the Swiss economic landscape. According to data released by the Swiss Insurance Association (SIA) as part of its annual sector survey, in 2025 the number of insured companies rose to 72,000, marking a 7% increase compared to the previous year. Even more sustained is the progression recorded among private clients, where the percentage growth reaches 18%, bringing the total to 480,000 active policies. From a financial volume perspective, the SIA survey highlights that collected premiums reached 29 million CHF for private clients, while the business sector generated a volume of 153 million CHF. This dynamic allows the sector to firmly establish itself among the fastest-growing within the Swiss insurance coverage market, responding to a demand for protection that evolves in parallel with the digitalization of commercial processes and daily life.
### The situation of companies and SMEs in the Swiss market
Despite the general increase in volumes and subscriptions, significant structural differences remain among the various types of businesses operating nationally. SIA findings reveal that only about 11% of Swiss companies are currently covered by insurance against cyber risks. Analyzing the distribution of this data, it clearly emerges that the greatest gaps are particularly concentrated among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which show lower adoption rates compared to large structures. Conversely, well over half of large companies already have specific coverage to handle any digital incidents or system blocks. This disproportion highlights how the widespread economic fabric, consisting predominantly of smaller entities, has not yet fully bridged the protection gap despite the growing exposure to cyber threats that characterizes the current Swiss economic context. The in-depth analysis conducted by the Swiss Insurance Association highlights that the cyber risk coverage sector plays a strategic role not only in safeguarding company balance sheets following an attack, but also in improving overall operational security. Swiss SMEs, while representing the segment with the greatest coverage gaps, are paradoxically those that could derive the greatest benefits from the assistance services associated with these policies. In addition to direct financial compensation for damages suffered following a cyber incident, insurance contracts regularly include targeted preventive services and the possibility of rapidly activating the support of experts specialized in digital emergency management. Heidi Fröhlich, head of non-life and reinsurance at the SIA, emphasizes that cyber insurance contributes significantly to strengthening the cyber resilience of companies, acting as a fundamental pillar in corporate risk management.
### The impact of cyber risks and upcoming institutional appointments
Cyber attacks currently constitute one of the most significant dangers to the business continuity of Swiss companies, surpassing many traditional threats in complexity and frequency. To address this evolution of risk and encourage dialogue between industry operators, institutions, and businesses, the sector's agenda includes targeted in-depth sessions. Among these, the Cyber Insurance Summit 2026 stands out, an important symposium entirely dedicated to the topic of digital protection and insurance coverage, scheduled for next November 5 in the city of Bern. The event will bring together experts and market representatives to analyze evolutionary trends, new types of cyber threats, and the most effective solutions to bridge the persistent protection gaps that continue to affect the national economic fabric, with particular attention paid to the specific needs of smaller business structures operating in Swiss territory.

## In brief - Stable apprenticeship market in 2026 - Around 76,000 apprenticeship contracts signed by the end of August - WorldSkills World Championships in Shanghai from September 22 to 27 - 42 young professionals in the SwissSkills national team
## Key facts - Press release date: September 17, 2026 - Apprenticeship contracts: approximately 76,000 - Survey: Transition Barometer - Polling institute: gfs.bern on behalf of SBFI - Survey publication: end of October 2026 - International event: WorldSkills Shanghai 2026 - WorldSkills edition: 48th - WorldSkills dates: September 22 to 27, 2026 - World talents: approximately 1,400 - Swiss delegation: 42 young professionals and 38 experts
The apprenticeship market in Switzerland is proving stable throughout 2026, with around 76,000 signed contracts recorded at the end of August. This figure confirms the strength of Swiss vocational education and training, demonstrating how companies continue to invest concretely in the new generation, offering young people important opportunities to enter the job world and significant career prospects. The observed stability continues in line with the volumes of previous years, highlighting a solid educational structure rooted in the country's economic fabric.
### The Transition Barometer and annual surveys To obtain an in-depth and detailed picture of the situation throughout 2026, observers and professionals refer to the Transition Barometer. This specific survey is conducted every year at two distinct times, precisely in the months of April and August. Through targeted surveys directed directly at young people and companies, the tool detects the latest developments characterising the delicate transition phase from compulsory schooling to upper secondary level II. The results of the survey conducted in August, carried out by the gfs.bern institute on behalf of SBFI, will be made public at the end of October 2026, providing further metrics on enrollment trends and youth employment tendencies nationwide. The relevance of Swiss vocational education and training is not limited to the domestic market, but also finds resonance and recognition on the international scene thanks to top-tier competitions. From September 22 to 27, 2026, the city of Shanghai will host the 48th edition of the WorldSkills professional championships. In this important global showcase, approximately 1,400 talents from all over the world will compete in a wide range of professional disciplines, offering a concrete demonstration of their technical and operational skills on a premier international stage.
### The Swiss Delegation and Global Competition Switzerland is participating in the international event with the SwissSkills 2026 national team, composed of 42 highly qualified young professionals. Accompanying and supporting the Swiss delegation in this adventure in Shanghai are 38 industry experts. Events of this international magnitude make it possible to highlight the structural strengths of the Swiss educational model, characterized by the close link between classroom theory and daily practice in the workplace, the high quality of the teaching provided, and constant cooperation between the Confederation, the Cantons, and organizations in the world of work. For the young professionals in competition, direct comparison with peers from other nations represents not only a rigorous test of their technical capabilities, but also an experience of personal and professional growth of inestimable value.
